prompt: Top-down merge sort on 1,024 elements has 10 levels of merging. You double the input to 2,048 elements. What happens to the number of merge levels and the total merging work?

options.text: One more level (11), so the total work slightly more than doubles
options.explanation: Correct. Halving 2,048 reaches single elements after 11 halvings instead of 10, and every level still touches every element: 2,048 elements on 11 levels against 1,024 on 10, about 2.2 times the work.

options.text: Twice as many levels (20), so the work roughly quadruples
options.explanation: The depth grows with the logarithm of the input size, not in proportion to it. Doubling the input adds one halving, not ten.

options.text: Still 10 levels; only the merges get longer, so the work exactly doubles
options.explanation: The merges do get longer, but 2,048 elements need one extra halving to reach single elements, so there is also one more level.

options.text: The work quadruples, like a quadratic sort
options.explanation: That is how insertion sort behaves on random input. Merge sort's work is linear per level with logarithmically many levels, so doubling the input only slightly more than doubles it.

workedExample:
1. Each level halves the subproblem size, and merging happens on every level above the single elements.
2. 1,024 elements reach size 1 after 10 halvings. 2,048 needs one more halving first (2,048 to 1,024), so it has 11 levels.
3. Every level touches every element once, so the work is roughly elements times levels: about 10,000 element moves for 1,024 elements and about 22,500 for 2,048.

Doubling the input therefore costs a little over twice the work. A quadratic sort would take about four times as long; that gap widens every time the input doubles.

prompt:
You run plain top-down merge sort (no extra checks) on an array of 1 million elements that is **already sorted**. What is its running time?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Θ(n), because the input is sorted
options.explanation: That requires an adaptive algorithm (like Timsort or merge sort with a 'skip if already in order' check). Plain merge sort still splits and merges everything.

Correct. Plain merge sort on n elements always does a base-two logarithmic number of merging levels (about 20 for a million); on sorted input each merge does fewer comparisons (about half), but it is still Θ(n log n).

options.text: Θ(n²), because sorted input is its worst case
options.explanation: That is quicksort with a first or last pivot. Merge sort always splits in the middle, so input order can't unbalance it.
Every element must at least be looked at, so no sort can be faster than Θ(n).

workedExample:
1. Merge sort always splits at the midpoint, regardless of the data. So the recursion tree always has about 20 levels for a million elements.
2. On sorted input, each merge of two halves makes as many comparisons as one half has elements (the left half empties first), rather than up to one fewer than both halves together. That roughly halves the comparisons but leaves all the copying.
3. Total: about half a comparison and one copy per element on each of about 20 levels: roughly 10 million comparisons plus 20 million element copies. That is still Θ(n log n), growing like n times log n.

A no-copy index-range implementation can skip ordered merges in Θ(n) total time. The shown slicing/concatenating implementation still copies Θ(n log n) elements.
